text: A function is a named, reusable block of code — write the logic once, run it as many times as you need with different inputs instead of copy-pasting the same lines everywhere. Today covers declaring one, parameters and arguments, default parameter values, function declarations versus function expressions, and the one thing about return values that trips up every beginner at least once.

A function takes parameters — placeholders it expects to receive, like name in a greet function. The actual values passed in when it's called are the arguments — so calling greet with the text 'Ana' passes 'Ana' as the argument for that parameter. return sends a value back out to wherever the function was called from, and everything written after return inside that same function never runs.

A default parameter value is used automatically whenever the caller doesn't pass that argument at all — call greet with no argument and it falls back to 'friend' instead of crashing or returning undefined. This becomes genuinely useful once a function takes several optional settings, which is extremely common in real code, especially in blockchain libraries with many configuration options.

A function declaration can be called earlier in the file than where it's written, because JavaScript moves it — hoists it — to the top of its scope before anything runs. A function expression stored in a variable cannot be called early; the variable itself doesn't exist yet at that point in the file. Both forms behave identically once they're actually defined — hoisting is the only practical difference.

Here's the trap: a function with no return statement doesn't return nothing, it returns undefined, every single time, silently, with no error or warning. If a value shows up as undefined somewhere you expected real data, the very first thing to check is whether the function that produced it simply forgot to return.

You're ready for lesson six when you can write a function with a default parameter, and explain exactly what it returns if you forget the return keyword. Parameters and arguments, default values, declarations versus expressions, and the silent undefined return. Next up: arrays and objects — how you actually structure real data.
